(Too sound of mind) The paper table cloth was tastefully bleak, The misty morning light shone on his cheek, And made him look alone and masculine. He talked of Seneca and bad translations, Of modern critics' lightweight observations; A bread crumb rested sweetly on his chin. Behind him, through the glass, the ocean's heave Uncurled against the sand, beside his sleeve, As Eros aimed his toxic javelin. I ducked out of the way, to no avail; It glanced my flesh, injecting quite a cocktail That blurred my sight and caused my head to spin— Never mind the coffee we were drinking, Whatever I said was not what I was thinking. I wanted to become his mandolin, And lie across his lap, a dainty lute, And sing to him and feed him ripened fruit, While light upon the sea turned opaline. Instead, this conversation about art And formal education—God, he's smart! Such rationality should be a sin. The hour was up, he had to run, of course; A handshake and a peck of shy remorse— Outside, the sea was gray and dull as tin; It ruled the shore with tedious discipline.

**(Too Sound of Mind)**

The paper tablecloth was tastefully bleak,
The misty morning light fell on his cheek,
And made him look aloof and masculine.
He spoke of Seneca and clumsy translations,
Of modern critics' lightweight observations;
A single breadcrumb rested on his chin.

Behind him, through the glass, the ocean's heave
Uncurled against the sand beside his sleeve,
As Eros aimed his toxic javelin.
I ducked to dodge its flight, but to no avail;
It grazed my flesh, injecting such a cocktail
As blurred my sight and set my head to spin—

Forget the very coffee we were drinking;
Whatever words I spoke were not my thinking.
I longed to be transformed—his mandolin—
To lie across his lap, a dainty lute,
And sing to him, and feed him ripened fruit,
While light upon the water turned opaline.

Instead, this measured discourse upon art
And formal education—God, he's smart!
Such perfect reason ought to be a sin.
The hour was up; he had to run, of course—
A handshake, and a peck of shy remorse—
Outside, the sea lay gray and dull as tin,
And ruled the shore with tedious discipline.

---

I also smoothed "I ducked out of the way" into "I ducked to dodge its flight" to sharpen the rhythm. Let me know if you'd prefer a lighter or bolder revision.

**(Perfectly Composed)**

The disposable placemat was elegantly plain,
While hazy dawn light gilded his face with a gentle stain,
Lending him a solitary, virile air.
He spoke of Seneca and clumsy renderings,
Of how today's reviewers offer only shallow things;
A speck of bread sat charming in his beard's soft hair.

Beyond him, past the window, waves rose up and fell,
Unfolding on the beach beside his cuff as well,
The moment Cupid drew his poisoned dart to bear.
I dodged aside, but still it found its mark;
It grazed my skin and pumped a mixture, potent, stark,
That fogged my vision, left my mind unclear—

Forget the coffee sitting there between us cooling,
For all my spoken words were nothing but my fooling.
I longed to be transformed into his stringed guitar,
To rest across his knees, a delicate small lute,
And serenade him, offer him some sun-warmed fruit,
As ocean glimmer shifted toward a milky star.

But no—this discourse turned to art instead,
And proper schooling—Lord, the mind inside his head!
That kind of clear-eyed reason ought to be forbidden.
Our time expired, and naturally he had to dash;
A parting handshake, one bashful kiss, then gone in a flash—
Beyond the door, the sea lay flat and drab as pewter,
Commanding all the coastline with a dull, exacting rigor.

# Across the Table

We sat across from one another in the pale, bleak light of morning, and I found myself admiring him—an intelligent man, unmistakably masculine, speaking with quiet authority. He talked of Seneca, of the delicate art of translation, of the modern critics and their various failings. There was something compelling in the way he moved through these subjects, as if each idea were a stone he turned over in his hands before setting it down.

He spoke of art and of formal education, and I listened, or seemed to. But somewhere in the middle of his careful reasoning, I was struck—suddenly, without warning—by desire. It came like a wound, as though Eros himself had hurled his poisoned javelin straight into me, and I had no defense against it.

The attraction was so overwhelming that it bent everything out of shape. My perception blurred; my words came out crooked. What I said bore no resemblance to what churned beneath—I heard myself speaking of translations while my mind wandered somewhere else entirely.

For I had begun to imagine myself transformed into his instrument. I saw myself lying across his lap, singing softly to him, lifting fruit to his mouth with my own fingers. And all the while our conversation continued, cool and rational, two composed voices exchanging measured thoughts, as though nothing at all were happening beneath the surface.

Then it was over. A handshake—formal, correct—and a shy goodbye. That was all. And I was left alone with the sea and the shore, both of them gone gray now, dull and flat and disappointing, ordinary as they had never seemed before.

# The Little Words That Hold Us Together

Some words are so small and so common that we hardly notice them at all. Take three of them: **"The," "And,"** and **"Too."** They rarely stand in the spotlight, yet without them, our language would fall apart.

## The

"The" is the quiet gatekeeper of the English language. It points, it specifies, it tells us exactly which thing we mean. There is a difference between *a* book and *the* book—the second one matters, it is known, it is chosen. "The" gives shape to the world by drawing a circle around what we already understand. It is the most used word in English, and yet most people never pause to appreciate how much work it does.

## And

"And" is the great connector. It links ideas, joins people, and stitches thoughts together into something larger than their parts. Bread and butter. Now and forever. You and I. Wherever there is a relationship, a partnership, or a list of things worth gathering, "and" is there, holding the pieces in place. It refuses to let anything stand entirely alone.

## Too

"Too" is the word of inclusion and excess. It can mean "also," welcoming one more into the group—*"I want to come, too."* Or it can signal that we have gone past a limit—*"too much," "too far," "too late."* In its small frame, it carries both belonging and warning, generosity and caution.

## Together

The, and, too—three humble words. Yet notice how they work together, and how much they carry, too. They remind us that meaning often lives not in the grand and dramatic words, but in the small ones we take for granted every single day.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem about falling suddenly in love with someone during a coffee date, using the imagery of Eros and his arrow. Make it witty and slightly self-mocking, with the ocean visible in the background.
counterfactuals.output:
Ambush at the Café by the Sea

I ordered black. I meant it, too—
a bitter man, a bitter brew,
immune to spring, immune to spring,
a cynic and a hardened thing.

And then you laughed. And then—the fool—
some winged and diapered little ghoul
took aim from where the sugar sat
and shot me somewhere near the cravat.

Eros, must you work like this?
Between the foam and cheese and bliss?
I'd built my walls with care and mortar;
you breached them over lukewarm water.

I tried to speak of tides and weather—
the ocean stitching sky to leather,
the gulls, the salt, the distant boat—
but all my clever caught my throat.

You mentioned you preferred oat milk.
My knees dissolved to something silk.
Absurd! I'm forty! This is treason!
I fell in love without a reason.

The waves came in. The waves withdrew.
I sat there, punctured, staring at you,
a grown man felled by tiny archery,
undone beside a plate of pastry.

So here I am, both smug and slain,
that little god's ridiculous stain,
still nursing coffee gone stone cold—
too struck to drink, too shy, too bold.

The sea keeps time. The arrow's set.
I have no dignity left. And yet—
would you, perhaps, when this is through,
allow me one more date with you?
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a formal rhyming poem where the speaker is smitten by an intellectual man discussing Seneca and literary criticism, but is too infatuated to focus on the conversation.
counterfactuals.output:
**On Being Poorly Schooled in Seneca**

He speaks of Seneca with gentle heat,
Of Stoic calm and how the ancients wrote;
I watch the way his lips shape each conceit
And lose the argument he means to quote.

He cites some critic's clever, cutting phrase,
Then leans to make his subtle point more clear—
I only mark the candor of his gaze
And let his careful reasoning disappear.

"You see," he says, "the tragic form demands
A moral weight the moderns have forgone."
I nod as though I follow where he stands,
Yet all his learned Latin passes on.

He parses grief and pity, guilt and pride,
The proper measure of a well-turned line;
But I am parsing only how he sighed,
And whether such a man could ever be mine.

He asks me, warm, what I have lately read—
And I, who cannot recollect a word,
Confess with burning cheek and lowered head
That every clever thing he said, I heard

As music with no meaning I could keep,
A tide of sound too lovely to divide.
He smiles. Perhaps he sees me in too deep;
Perhaps he, too, has set his books aside.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.output:
# Table for One, Perhaps

"How is your coffee?" — steam curls past your lips,
the cinnamon a ghost between us two.
I watch the winter light in amber sips
and say the rain seems likely. (I mean *you.*)

The espresso hisses, bitter, dark, and true;
a saucer clinks its small porcelain applause.
"More sugar?" No—I've swallowed something new,
a syllable I hold behind my jaws.

Your laughter warms the window's frosted glass.
I trace the ring your cup left, wet and round,
and speak of trains, of how the seasons pass,
while every word I want stays underground.

You gather coat and gloves. The bell rings clear.
"Take care," I smile—and mean *God, stay right here.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poem where mythological love (Cupid/Eros) collides with modern everyday reality—a mundane coffee meeting by the sea—and the speaker fantasizes about becoming the beloved's musical instrument.
counterfactuals.output:
# Eros at the Espresso Bar

You stir your coffee like it's nothing,
like the sea behind you isn't ancient,
like Eros didn't set up shop
between the sugar packets and the foam.

I watch your fingers on the ceramic—
absent, tapping some private rhythm—
and the old god pulls his string so quietly
I mistake the wound for weather.

The gulls are shameless. So am I.

Make me the cello propped against your knee,
the curve of wood you'd lean into and never notice
you were playing. Let your careless hands
find the frets they didn't know they longed for.
I would hold the tension of your tuning.
I would ache in every register you asked of me.

But here the myth just orders another latte.

Cupid, drunk on salt air and the thin foam
you leave clinging to your lip,
has traded arrows for the small talk
of a Tuesday, for the way you say *the water's cold this time of year*
and mean nothing, and undo me.

I am not the reed you'd bring to your mouth.
I am not the harp against your collarbone.
I am the man across the table
learning that desire, uncomposed,
is just two people and the tide
and a bill neither of us reaches for,

while somewhere in my chest
a string I didn't string
goes on and on and on—

and you, oblivious virtuoso,
finish your drink
and ask me if I'm ready to go.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a clever, ironic love poem in rhymed lines about being intellectually attracted to a "too smart" man, ending with the disappointment of the date ending and the sea turning dull and gray.
counterfactuals.output:
**Too Clever by Half**

You quoted Kant before we'd ordered wine,
And parsed my laughter into rhyme and reason;
I fell for footnotes in that voice of thine,
Mistaking cleverness for love's sweet season.

You knew the name of every distant star,
The Latin root of every word I said,
You calculated just how wrong we are—
Then proved it, twice, inside my dizzy head.

I loved the way you argued I was wrong,
And made my blushing seem a syllogism;
You turned my sighing into evensong
And every kiss into a criticism.

So brilliant, dear, you analyzed the spark
Until the poor thing shivered, then expired;
You lectured on the physics of the dark
While I sat waiting, foolishly, to be desired.

The bill arrived; you calculated tip
To seven digits, precise and refined,
Then, quoting Proust, you let the evening slip—
And left me smarter, lonelier, behind.

I walked the shore where wit could not console,
Where all your theorems turned to salt and spray;
The clever tide withdrew, and took its toll—
And so the sea turned dull, and dim, and gray.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
